approved: Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Tax Integrity) Bill 2017

The speaker argued the government's housing tax integrity bills are minor, ineffective tinkering that will not improve affordability, and contrasted them with Labor's plan to reform negative gearing and capital gains tax. The bills disallow travel expense deductions for rental properties, limit plant and equipment deductions, and impose a vacancy fee on foreign owners, measures the speaker called a "sham" without substantial reform.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Tax Integrity) Bill 2017, arguing it improves housing affordability through three targeted reforms: removing travel expense deductions for investors (saving $540 million), limiting depreciation claims to original purchasers, and imposing a vacancy charge on foreign-owned empty properties. He criticised Labor’s proposed removal of negative gearing and capital gains concessions as a dangerous one-size-fits-all approach that would crash property prices and destabilise rental markets.

The speaker supported the bills as integrity measures but argued they do not go far enough, criticising the government for refusing to reform negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount, which they said fuel unaffordable house prices—noting a 46% price increase in Malabar and similar rises in Coogee. They announced Labor’s alternative policy to restrict negative gearing to new housing, halve the capital gains tax discount, and introduce a vacant property tax, claiming it would create 25,000 jobs per year and 55,000 new homes over three years.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Tax Integrity) Bill 2017 and the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Fees Imposition Amendment (Vacancy Fees) Bill 2017 will improve rental market integrity by disallowing travel expense deductions for rental property visits and preventing depreciation claims on assets included in property purchases. The speaker also announced that foreign investors must rent out new properties for at least six months a year or face vacancy fees (e.g., $5,500 for a $600,000 property, $22,300 for a $2 million property), and noted the coalition has ordered 61 forced sales of illegally acquired properties totalling over $107 million.

The speaker argued that the government's housing affordability bills are ineffective and that any genuine solution must include reforms to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount. The speaker supported an amendment by the member for McMahon stating that a housing package without these reforms is a sham, and criticised the government's First Home Super Saver Scheme for potentially worsening affordability and undermining superannuation.

The bill disallows travel expense deductions for residential property investors (saving $540 million), limits plant and equipment depreciation deductions to new assets only (saving $260 million), and introduces an annual vacancy charge on foreign-owned residential properties that are not occupied or rented for at least six months.
